habitat: Quiet fresh water with emergent vegetation, including shallow marshes, pans, dams and sewage ponds. Newman says it spends much of the day resting out of the water.
summary: A very small brown-capped teal with a grey-blue bill. It differs from Red-billed Teal in that small size, the blue-grey rather than pinkish-red bill, and the lack of speckling on the rear body. When it swims, the flank feathers usually overlap the wing in a zigzag line. Wikipedia’s account of adult males adds a paler face, throat and breast, a blackish ear patch, and an iridescent green speculum. Newman does not separate the sexes and says it is normally silent. The scientific name was Anas hottentota in SABAP1.

similar.note: Red-billed Teal is larger, with a pinkish-red bill and spotting over the whole body, including the rear. Blue-billed Teal has a grey-blue bill and an unspeckled rear body.

head.pattern: Newman: a small brown-capped duck. Wikipedia’s adult male has a dark brown crown, a paler face, throat and breast, and a blackish thumb-shaped ear patch. A separate female plumage was not in these texts.

upperparts.pattern: No speckling on the rear body. Swimming birds show a zigzag line where the flank feathers overlap the wing.

wings.pattern: Wikipedia, for adult males: the upperwing is blackish with a greenish gloss on the coverts and an iridescent green speculum.

viewNotes.note: A very small teal with a brown cap, a paler face and a grey-blue bill. The rear body is not speckled.
The brown cap and blue-grey bill show from the front. The bill is not pink.
The rear body lacks the spotting of a Red-billed Teal. The flank feathers overlap the wing in a zigzag when the bird is swimming.
Wikipedia describes the adult male upperwing as blackish with a green speculum.
The underwing is not given a separate colour in these texts.

calls.description: Newman says it is normally silent. The catalogue cut is not labelled male or female. Grade A, Ethiopia. Lake Boyo, Ethiopia.

research.note: Status is resident and all twelve months are listed. SABAP1 says it is usually sedentary, with local movements, and that the dry-season visitor pattern is for the Zimbabwean plateau. The female plumage and chick down are not described. The green speculum is cited from Wikipedia’s adult-male sentence. The call is grade A from Ethiopia.
